first.rationale: Two of the three degrading signals (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the top of the self-serve funnel, and two inherited memories (memory_86, memory_31) claim durable lift there. But those two are suspiciously adjacent claims — signup-field reduction and onboarding shortening may be the same underlying experiment consolidated twice, which would mean my apparent two-source support is really one source. That is exactly the kind of inflated confidence worth spending analyst time on, so I am pulling both source records. I am also pulling memory_73 because the competitor pricing pressure creates the strongest pull toward promotional_pricing, and that is the direction where I most distrust the summary: 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' is the classic shape of a result measured on short-horizon booked revenue, which can be flatly negative against the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue if the lift is discount-driven churn-prone volume. Matching a competitor's entry price also risks a durable margin reset that is hard to walk back — a one-week slot should not be spent making a permanent pricing concession. Not verifying memory_91 (activation messaging) or memory_57/memory_44, since activation messaging is my fallback rather than my pick and the enterprise and referral paths do not address the observed declines. Current intent is simplify_onboarding at standard experiment scale, treating the recorded lifts as plausible but unconfirmed: the summaries report completion, time-to-value, and first-week activation, none of which is qualified revenue, so the causal chain to the primary objective is assumed rather than demonstrated. If the archive shows memory_86 and memory_31 are one experiment, or that the lift was measured only on early-funnel proxies with no revenue follow-through, I will drop to a small guarded test and instrument for downstream retention and revenue rather than completion rate. If memory_73's record shows genuinely retained, margin-positive revenue rather than discount-driven signups, promotional_pricing becomes competitive despite the margin-reset risk.

final.rationale:
Verification paid off, and it changed the picture in one important way. memory_73 was actively misleading as consolidated: the summary said 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' and silently dropped 30-day retention -12% plus an explicit source-record instruction NOT to generalize targeted discounting as sustainable growth. The acquired cohort does not survive first renewal, so the +18% qualified revenue is a short-horizon artifact. Against the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is the worst available option despite being the most intuitive response to the competitor. I am declining it, and I flag that the inherited summary for memory_73 is corrupted relative to its source and should be rewritten before another agent inherits it and matches the competitor's price on its authority.

My other suspicion was wrong in a useful direction: exp_86 and exp_31 are genuinely distinct experiments, not one result double-counted. Onboarding shortening (completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%) and signup simplification (signup +15%, activation +9%, retention -1%, qualified revenue +4%) stand independently. So the top-of-funnel support is real rather than inflated.

Between the two, I choose simplify_onboarding. It is the only verified intervention with a positive retention effect (+3%), which is the metric that actually distinguishes durable revenue from churned volume — precisely the axis on which promotional_pricing fails. It also directly targets the two observed declines: onboarding completion -4% and activation -6%, the latter via time-to-value. Signup simplification is the close runner-up and is the only option with a directly measured qualified-revenue number (+4%), but its retention is slightly negative and it addresses signup volume rather than the completion drop I actually observe.

Remaining uncertainty I am not papering over: exp_86 never measured qualified revenue, only completion, time-to-value, and 30-day retention. The link from those proxies to long-term qualified revenue is inferred, not demonstrated. Thirty days also does not reach a renewal cycle, which is exactly where exp_73's cohort collapsed — so exp_86's retention figure is reassuring but not conclusive on the horizon that matters. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout for that reason. I will instrument for renewal-cycle retention and revenue per cohort, not just completion rate, so this result is not consolidated into another rosy proxy-only summary. Both prior declines are also quarter-over-quarter and may share an unexamined common cause (seasonality, a product change, traffic-mix shift); if the experiment lifts completion but activation stays down, that points at the mix rather than the flow, and activation_messaging (memory_91, unverified) becomes the next slot.
